Meeting Header:
Date: 2025-03-18
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~56 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Jordan Reyes (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Maya Chen (Redwood SE), Claire Zhang (VectorMetrics Head of ML), Tom Alvarez (SRE), Priya Nair (Data Scientist), Ethan Brooks (Product)

Auto-generated Summary: Deep dive on embeddings + reranking perf, discussing vector dims, batch sizes, target latency SLOs, and cost estimates. Action items and POC plan agreed.

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan: ok hey everyone thanks for joining today, um this is a technical deep dive on embeddings and reranking. i'll let samir kick off with the perf overview.
[00:18] Samir: yeah thanks jordan. hi claire, team. quick agenda: we wanted to cover vector dims (512/768/1536), batching strategy, latency targets - you mentioned p95 under 50ms - kv cache usage for rerank, and quantization options for cost savings.
[00:40] Claire: yep that's right, p95 ideally under 50ms for online reranking, throughput about 200 qps, and cost is a big factor. we run a two-stage pipeline: dense retrieval then rerank top-100.
[01:05] Maya: thanks, helpful. can you confirm the distribution of query lengths and candidate counts?
[01:12] Priya: most queries are short, 8-16 tokens, candidates per query currently 100-200, but for the POC we'll start at 100.
[01:30] Samir: great. from Redwood's side, reranking typically uses embeddings to compute similarity then a small transformer for cross-encoder scores. for embedding-based rerank we focus on vector dimension vs recall/latency tradeoffs.
[01:50] Tom: any rule of thumb on dims? we've heard 1536 is more accurate but more costly.
[01:58] Samir: yeah so 512 gives you good baseline for many use cases, 768 is a sweet spot, and 1536/2048 give better recall on hard queries but cost and latency increase ~linear with dim. rough numbers - on our infra a 512-d vector cosine sim is ~x2 faster than 1536 for pure dot-product ops due to memory bandwidth and cache locality.
[02:25] Claire: and for reranking the second stage, does it use the same embedding dims or a separate cross-encoder?
[02:32] Samir: both patterns exist. for pure embedding rerank, you can embed candidates and queries and compute sims. for cross-encoder rerank we run an attention model over concatenated query+candidate which is heavier - higher latency; often we do embedding first then cross-encoder on top-k.
[02:55] Jordan: quick interruption - when you say "cross-encoder" for top-k 100, what's the per-request latency ballpark?
[03:03] Samir: depends on model size and quantization. a small cross-encoder quantized to 4-bit can do ~80-120ms p95 for a single candidate on GPU if run serially, but with batching and model fusion we can amortize. that's why embedding-first is common.
[03:25] Priya: hmm 80-120ms per candidate would blow our SLO. we need a plan that keeps rerank p95 under 50ms end-to-end.
[03:33] Samir: understood. two main levers: reduce top-k passed to cross-encoder (e.g., 20 instead of 100), use efficient cross-encoder architectures, and leverage batch scoring and KV cache where applicable.
[03:50] Maya: also quantization: 8-bit or 4-bit weights can reduce memory and increase throughput, but sometimes accuracy drops. we usually suggest running a small eval to measure quality delta.
[04:10] Claire: what's your experience with KV cache for rerank? priya's team wondered if we can cache candidate embeddings.
[04:18] Samir: absolutely. KV cache is most often discussed for autoregressive decoding, but prefix/candidate embedding caching is a critical win for rerank. if your candidate corpus is relatively static, cache embeddings in Redis/Pinecone/FAISS and avoid recomputing. Redwood also supports in-flight KV caching in the serving runtime for repeated prefixes which helps scoring reuse.
[04:45] Tom: are there consistency concerns with cache invalidation? we do frequent document updates.
[04:51] Samir: yes you'll need TTLs or invalidate on updates; for our Dedicated customers we support a hook to invalidate keys via API. also batching candidate embedding computation helps catch up during index updates.
[05:10] Priya: batch sizes - what's the recommended batch for embeddings? our current pipeline batches 8 at a time to keep latency low.
[05:18] Samir: batch size tradeoff: small batches (1-8) favor latency; large batches (32-128) favor throughput and cost. on GPUs, throughput increases sublinearly - e.g., 32->128 might get you 2-3x throughput but p95 latency will increase. for your p95 50ms SLO at 200 qps, we typically recommend batching queries across shards and using async inference paths; for embedding generation we see p95 ~20-40ms for 512-d at batch 8 on our optimized runtime; 1536-d at batch 8 is closer to 60-80ms p95.
[05:55] Jordan: note that latency above ~60ms for embedding phase will push end-to-end beyond your target if you still do cross-encoder.
[06:03] Claire: what about quantized embeddings? like compute in 8-bit then convert?
[06:08] Samir: you can quantize model weights and still produce FP32 embeddings; quantization affects compute and memory but numerical fidelity sometimes degrades similarity scores slightly. common approach: run eval on your labeled data to measure MRR/Recall drop; often 8-bit is safe, 4-bit sometimes requires per-layer calibration.
[06:30] Priya: do you support QAT or PTQ?
[06:33] Maya: we support post-training quantization (PTQ) in the runtime and recommend tuning per-model. QAT is possible but more involved.
[06:42] Tom: cost estimates - can you ballpark cost per million queries for embedding + rerank?
[06:47] Samir: ballpark: hosted embeddings-only flow might be $X-$Y per 1M depending on dim and batching; with dedicated and aggressive batching/quantization, you can reduce unit cost by 2-4x. (note: we captured placeholders; we'll send a detailed pricing sheet).
[07:10] Claire: ok please send concrete numbers.
[07:13] Jordan: will do, we'll attach a benchmark spreadsheet.
[07:20] Priya: network and VPC - we need on-prem or VPC peering for compliance. if we run Dedicated in our cloud VPC, can you explain the network path and expected added latency?
[07:31] Samir: yes running Dedicated in your VPC via peering or PrivateLink adds minimal ms-level network latency; the bigger impact is TLS termination and routing. for on-prem air-gapped setups latency depends on your hardware. we usually recommend colocating inference near your retrieval store to avoid cross-region hops.
[07:55] Tom: firewall rules - what ports and egress rules are needed?
[07:59] Jordan: we'll send a checklist, but typically HTTPS outbound to Redwood control plane for telemetry, and internal gRPC between nodes for performance. Dedicated also has optional offline package.
[08:12] Claire: benchmarks - can you run our dataset?
[08:15] Samir: yes that's the plan. we'll run 3 dims (512/768/1536), batch sizes [8,32,128], and top-k values [20,50,100], measure p50/p95/p99 and throughput. we'll also test quantized model variants (8-bit, 4-bit) and compute embedding recall and rerank MRR.
[08:40] Priya: how will you handle candidate corpus in the POC? we'll provide a 50k candidate set.
[08:45] Samir: perfect. we'll index candidates in FAISS on the Dedicated cluster and optionally test external vector store like Pinecone to compare.
[08:55] Maya: one caveat: approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) search introduces recall/latency variance; if you need deterministic recall, we can run exhaustive but it's slower.
[09:10] Ethan: any tips on reducing p99 tail latencies?
[09:14] Samir: common causes: noisy co-tenants, large batch packing variance, and cold KV cache misses. mitigation: reserved capacity (Dedicated), bounded batch sizes with SLO-aware routing, and prewarming caches.
[09:30] Priya: prewarming - how often do you refresh candidate embeddings?
[09:34] Samir: depends on update cadence; for frequent updates we recommend incremental reindexing and a short TTL on cache keys so misses are limited.
[09:45] Claire: regarding quantization impact on similarity metrics, do you have numbers?
[09:49] Samir: summary from past customers: 8-bit PTQ often results in <1-2% drop in recall for many models; 4-bit can be 3-5% unless you do per-layer calibration. but we will measure on your labels.
[10:05] Jordan: i'd also add model architecture matters - some models are more robust to low-bit quantization. we'll note that in the benchmark results.
[10:15] Tom: storage and memory for 1536-d candidate vectors - what's the estimate for 50k vectors?
[10:20] Samir: rough: 1536-d float32 ~ 1536*4 = ~6 KB per vector, so 50k is ~300 MB plus index overhead; with 8-bit or product quantization compressed size drops significantly.
[10:40] Priya: what's the runtime behavior if we do hybrid approach: embedding-based shortlist + cheap cross-encoder on top-20?
[10:46] Samir: that's common. embedding stage: produce top-200 in ~20-40ms (512-d) then cross-encoder on 20 items in a batched call - with quantization and batch size 20 you can often hit sub-50ms for the cross-encoder portion on a dedicated GPU if configured correctly.
[11:10] Claire: does Redwood support multi-model routing? e.g., cheap embedder for recall then a higher-precision embedder for hard cases?
[11:17] Maya: yes, smart routing can send requests by policy to different model variants, fall back to hosted if Dedicated is overloaded.
[11:28] Jordan: any security concerns for cust data when using cached embeddings?
[11:33] Samir: embedding vectors could be considered sensitive; we recommend encrypting at rest and using KMS-managed keys for Dedicated; VPC ensures network isolation. we'll include our SOC2 and encryption docs.
[11:50] Ethan: excellent. one more: latency SLO verification - can you instrument p95 alerts?
[11:55] Maya: yes Redwood Console provides p50/p95/p99 breakdowns per-route and token-level cost, and we can add tracing hooks to correlate tail with infra events.
[12:10] Claire: ok let's recap next steps.
[12:13] Jordan: samir will run benchmarks on the dataset (512/768/1536, batches 8/32/128, top-k 20/50/100) and share results. jordan will send pricing, security docs, and a pilot contract. customer to provide dataset and confirm network setup.
[12:30] Priya: sounds good. thanks everyone.
[12:35] (crosstalk) Tom: thanks, bye.
